Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

`src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. content.text:
Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Summary of the fix:
- **`src/dsu.js`**: Implemented `checkCount`/`checkElement` validation, added a `#history` array that records each union as `{ attached, root }`. `checkpoint()` returns `#history.length`; `undo()` pops the last entry and reverses it exactly (restore size, detach the parent pointer); `rollback(token)` validates the token and repeatedly calls `undo()` until history length matches it, returning the count undone.
- Critically, I **removed path compression** from `find()`. With compression, `find` could repoint several elements directly at a later root, and a subsequent `undo()` (which only resets one parent pointer) could no longer be a true inverse of `union` — this caused two test failures (broken partitions after undo). Since union-by-size alone already keeps `find` at O(log n), dropping compression preserves correctness of the exact-undo invariant without sacrificing needed performance for this test suite.
- **`src/kruskal.js`**: Added the same validation helpers (`checkCount`, `checkElement`, `checkEdges`), implemented `minimumSpanningForest` (sort by weight, then first/second endpoint; union via `DisjointSets`, collecting accepted edges and total weight), and `componentsWithAlternatives` (apply base edges once, take a checkpoint, then for each alternative: apply it, record `components`, and `rollback` to the checkpoint before trying the next one).

goal.objective:
Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Validate up front. A count that is not a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `count must be a non-negative integer`. An element that is not a safe integer in `0 .. count - 1` raises `RangeError` with message `element out of range: 7`, quoting the offending value. An edge list that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `edges must be an array`, an edge that is not a three-element array raises `TypeError` with message `edge must be [u, v, weight]`, a weight that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `weight must be a finite number`, and an alternatives argument that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `alternatives must be an array`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

content.text:
Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. 1: /**
2:  * An event-sourced double-entry ledger: accounts, immutable entries, balances
3:  * at any point in time, and reversals.
4:  */
5: import { ACCOUNT_TYPES, LedgerError, toNormal } from './money.js';
6: 
7: function isNonEmptyString(value) {
8:   return typeof value === 'string' && value !== '';
9: }
10: 
11: function isNonNegativeInteger(value) {
12:   return typeof value === 'number' && Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 0;
13: }

15: /** A ledger of accounts and the balanced entries posted against them. */
16: export class Ledger {
17:   #accounts = new Map();
18:   #entries = new Map();
19:   #order = [];
20:   #nextSeq = 1;
21: 
22:   /**
23:    * Open an account.
24:    *
25:    * @param {{id: string, name: string, type: string}} account Account to open.
26:    * @returns {Readonly<{id: string, name: string, type: string}>} The opened account.
27:    */
28:   openAccount(account) {
29:     if (typeof account !== 'object' || account === null) {
30:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ACCOUNT', 'account must be an object');
31:     }
32:     const { id, name, type } = account;
33:     if (typeof id !== 'string' || id === '') {
34:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ACCOUNT', 'account id must be a non-empty string');
35:     }
36:     if (typeof name !== 'string' || name === '') {
37:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ACCOUNT', 'account name must be a non-empty string');
38:     }
39:     if (!ACCOUNT_TYPES.includes(type)) throw new LedgerError('UNKNOWN_TYPE', `unknown account type: ${type}`);
40:     if (this.#accounts.has(id)) throw new LedgerError('DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT', `account already exists: ${id}`);
41:     const record = Object.freeze({ id, name, type });
42:     this.#accounts.set(id, record);
43:     return record;
44:   }
45: 
46:   /** @returns {Array<Readonly<object>>} Accounts in ascending id order. */
47:   accounts() {
48:     return [...this.#accounts.keys()].sort().map((id) => this.#accounts.get(id));
49:   }
50: 
51:   #requireAccount(accountId) {
52:     const account = this.#accounts.get(accountId);
53:     if (!account) throw new LedgerError('UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT', `unknown account: ${accountId}`);
54:     return account;
55:   }
56: 
57:   #expose(record) {
58:     return Object.freeze({
59:       id: record.id,
60:       at: record.at,
61:       seq: record.seq,
62:       memo: record.memo,
63:       lines: record.lines,
64:       reverses: record.reverses,
65:       reversedBy: record.reversedBy,
66:     });
67:   }
68: 
69:   /**
70:    * Internal entry poster shared by post() and reverse().
71:    *
72:    * @param {object} entry Raw entry payload.
73:    * @param {string|null} reversesId Entry id being reversed, if any.
74:    * @returns {Readonly<object>} The stored entry.
75:    */
76:   #post(entry, reversesId) {
77:     if (typeof entry !== 'object' || entry === null) {
78:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ENTRY', 'entry must be an object');
79:     }
80:     const { id, at, lines } = entry;
81:     const memo = entry.memo === undefined ? '' : entry.memo;
82: 
83:     if (!isNonEmptyString(id)) {
84:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ENTRY', 'entry id must be a non-empty string');
85:     }
86:     if (this.#entries.has(id)) {
87:       throw new LedgerError('DUPLICATE_ENTRY', `entry already exists: ${id}`);
88:     }
89:     if (!isNonNegativeInteger(at)) {
90:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_TIME', 'entry time must be a non-negative integer');
91:     }
92:     if (typeof memo !== 'string') {
93:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_ENTRY', 'entry memo must be a string');
94:     }
95:     if (!Array.isArray(lines) || lines.length < 2) {
96:       throw new LedgerError('TOO_FEW_LINES', 'entry must have at least two lines');
97:     }
98: 
99:     const validatedLines = [];
100:     let sum = 0;
101:     for (const line of lines) {
102:       const account = line && line.account;
103:       const amountCents = line && line.amountCents;
104:       this.#requireAccount(account);
105:       if (!Number.isSafeInteger(amountCents)) {
106:         throw new LedgerError('NOT_INTEGER', 'amountCents must be a safe integer');
107:       }
108:       if (amountCents === 0) {
109:         throw new LedgerError('ZERO_LINE', 'amountCents must not be zero');
110:       }
111:       sum += amountCents;
112:       validatedLines.push(Object.freeze({ account, amountCents }));
113:     }
114:     if (sum !== 0) {
115:       throw new LedgerError('UNBALANCED', 'entry lines must sum to zero');
116:     }
117: 
118:     let original = null;
119:     if (reversesId !== null) {
120:       original = this.#entries.get(reversesId);
121:       if (at < original.at) {
122:         throw new LedgerError('BAD_TIME', 'reversal must not precede its entry');
123:       }
124:     }
125: 
126:     const seq = this.#nextSeq;
127:     this.#nextSeq += 1;
128:     const record = {
129:       id,
130:       at,
131:       seq,
132:       memo,
133:       lines: Object.freeze(validatedLines),
134:       reverses: reversesId,
135:       reversedBy: null,
136:     };
137:     this.#entries.set(id, record);
138:     this.#order.push(record);
139:     if (original) {
140:       original.reversedBy = id;
141:     }
142:     return this.#expose(record);
143:   }
144: 
145:   /**
146:    * Post a balanced entry.
147:    *
148:    * @param {{id: string, at: number, memo?: string, lines: Array<{account: string, amountCents: number}>}} entry Entry to post.
149:    * @returns {Readonly<object>} The stored entry.
150:    */
151:   post(entry) {
152:     return this.#post(entry, null);
153:   }
154: 
155:   /**
156:    * Look up an entry.
157:    *
158:    * @param {string} id Entry id.
159:    * @returns {Readonly<object>|undefined} The entry, if it exists.
160:    */
161:   getEntry(id) {
162:     const record = this.#entries.get(id);
163:     return record ? this.#expose(record) : undefined;
164:   }
165: 
166:   #sortedEntries() {
167:     return [...this.#order].sort((a, b) => (a.at - b.at) || (a.seq - b.seq));
168:   }
169: 
170:   #checkAsOf(asOf) {
171:     if (asOf !== Infinity && !isNonNegativeInteger(asOf)) {
172:       throw new LedgerError('BAD_TIME', 'asOf must be a non-negative integer');
173:     }
174:   }
175: 
176:   /**
177:    * Entries up to a moment, oldest first.
178:    *
179:    * @param {{asOf?: number}} [options] Cut-off, inclusive.
180:    * @returns {Array<Readonly<object>>} Matching entries ordered by time then posting order.
181:    */
182:   entries(options = {}) {
183:     const asOf = options.asOf === undefined ? Infinity : options.asOf;
184:     this.#checkAsOf(asOf);
185:     return this.#sortedEntries()
186:       .filter((record) => record.at <= asOf)
187:       .map((record) => this.#expose(record));
188:   }
189: 
190:   /**
191:    * Debit-positive balance of one account.
192:    *
193:    * @param {string} accountId Account to measure.
194:    * @param {{asOf?: number}} [options] Cut-off, inclusive.
195:    * @returns {number} Signed balance in cents.
196:    */
197:   balance(accountId, options = {}) {
198:     this.#requireAccount(accountId);
199:     const asOf = options.asOf === undefined ? Infinity : options.asOf;
200:     this.#checkAsOf(asOf);
201:     let total = 0;
202:     for (const record of this.#order) {
203:       if (record.at > asOf) continue;
204:       for (const line of record.lines) {
205:         if (line.account === accountId) total += line.amountCents;
206:       }
207:     }
208:     return total;
209:   }
210: 
211:   /**
212:    * Balance of one account in its own normal direction.
213:    *
214:    * @param {string} accountId Account to measure.
215:    * @param {{asOf?: number}} [options] Cut-off, inclusive.
216:    * @returns {number} Balance in cents, positive when on the normal side.
217:    */
218:   normalBalance(accountId, options = {}) {
219:     const account = this.#requireAccount(accountId);
220:     const signed = this.balance(accountId, options);
221:     return toNormal(account.type, signed);
222:   }
223: 
224:   /**
225:    * Debit and credit totals across every account.
226:    *
227:    * @param {{asOf?: number}} [options] Cut-off, inclusive.
228:    * @returns {{debits: number, credits: number, byAccount: Record<string, number>}} Trial balance.
229:    */
230:   trialBalance(options = {}) {
231:     const asOf = options.asOf === undefined ? Infinity : options.asOf;
232:     this.#checkAsOf(asOf);
233:     let debits = 0;
234:     let credits = 0;
235:     const byAccount = {};
236:     for (const account of this.accounts()) {
237:       const value = this.balance(account.id, { asOf });
238:       byAccount[account.id] = value;
239:       if (value > 0) debits += value;
240:       else if (value < 0) credits += -value;
241:     }
242:     return { debits, credits, byAccount };
243:   }
244: 
245:   /**
246:    * Post the mirror image of an entry.
247:    *
248:    * @param {string} entryId Entry to reverse.
249:    * @param {{id: string, at: number, memo?: string}} options Identity and time of the reversal.
250:    * @returns {Readonly<object>} The reversing entry.
251:    */
252:   reverse(entryId, options) {
253:     const original = this.#entries.get(entryId);
254:     if (!original) throw new LedgerError('NOT_FOUND', `unknown entry: ${entryId}`);
255:     if (original.reverses !== null) throw new LedgerError('REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL', `entry is itself a reversal: ${entryId}`);
256:     if (original.reversedBy !== null) throw new LedgerError('ALREADY_REVERSED', `entry already reversed: ${entryId}`);
257: 
258:     const lines = original.lines.map((line) => ({ account: line.account, amountCents: -line.amountCents }));
259:     const memo = options && options.memo !== undefined ? options.memo : `reversal of ${entryId}`;
260:     const payload = { id: options && options.id, at: options && options.at, memo, lines };
261:     return this.#post(payload, entryId);
262:   }
263: 
264:   /**
265:    * Every line touching one account inside a window, with a running balance.
266:    *
267:    * @param {string} accountId Account to report on.
268:    * @param {{from?: number, to?: number}} [options] Inclusive window.
269:    * @returns {Array<{entryId: string, at: number, seq: number, amountCents: number, balanceCents: number}>} Statement rows.
270:    */
271:   statement(accountId, options = {}) {
272:     this.#requireAccount(accountId);
273:     const from = options.from === undefined ? -Infinity : options.from;
274:     const to = options.to === undefined ? Infinity : options.to;
275:     const rows = [];
276:     let running = 0;
277:     for (const record of this.#sortedEntries()) {
278:       for (const line of record.lines) {
279:         if (line.account !== accountId) continue;
280:         running += line.amountCents;
281:         if (record.at >= from && record.at <= to) {
282:           rows.push({
283:             entryId: record.id,
284:             at: record.at,
285:             seq: record.seq,
286:             amountCents: line.amountCents,
287:             balanceCents: running,
288:           });
289:         }
290:       }
291:     }
292:     return rows;
293:   }

goal.objective:
Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. `src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. Operations are checked before they run: a non-object operation throws `operation must be an object`, an unrecognised or missing `op` throws `unknown operation: frob`, and missing members throw `add requires a path`, `add requires a value` or `move requires a from`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. Keys that shadow `Object.prototype`, including `__proto__`, are ordinary own properties throughout: adding `/__proto__` must leave the result's prototype and every other object alone, and resolving `/toString` on an empty object must fail. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. - `add` inserts into arrays (`-` appends, index may equal length), `replace` on `''` swaps the whole document, `remove` on `''` throws, `move` is a no-op for equal pointers and rejects moving into its own child, `copy` inserts an independent copy, and `test` uses a recursive `jsonEqual` (order-insensitive members, ordered elements, no coercion).

`src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. `applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. content.text: OK: no node_modules

The `src/trie.js` implementation is complete and passing all tests.

Summary of what was done:
- Replaced the plain-map stub with a real trie (`TrieNode` per distinct prefix), keyed by Unicode code points via `[...string]` iteration so astral characters (like `\u{1F600}`) are single steps rather than surrogate-pair halves.

The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
I'll start by exploring the workspace.

12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;

What I implemented:

**`src/machine.js`** — a frozen `TRANSITIONS` table mapping each state to its ascending command list. `allowedTypes` throws `TypeError('unknown state: <state>')` for anything not in the table and returns a fresh copy so callers can mutate it freely; `isTerminal` simply reports whether that list is empty, so it agrees with `TERMINAL_STATES` by construction rather than by duplication.

**`src/order.js`** — `apply` runs the checks in the required order:

1. Structural validation throws `TypeError` before anything is recorded.
2. A known `commandId` returns the memoized result with `replayed: true`, touching nothing — the clock, audit and item list are all untouched.
3. A regressive `at` is rejected with `CLOCK_REGRESSION` and its audit entry is stamped with the current `clockMs`, so recorded times are monotone; every other command advances the clock.
4. `BAD_STATE`, then per-type field checks (`MISSING_FIELD` / `BAD_AMOUNT`), then business guards (`DUPLICATE_SKU`, `NO_SUCH_ITEM`, `EMPTY_ORDER`, `AMOUNT_MISMATCH`, `REFUND_TOO_LARGE`).

A single private `#record` helper appends the one audit entry, captures `to` after the effect has run (so rejections naturally get `from === to`), memoizes the result and hands back a copy — that is what keeps "exactly one entry per command that reaches the clock check" true on both the success and failure paths without repeating the bookkeeping.

Two details worth flagging: `refund` only moves to `refunded` once `refundedCents` reaches `paidCents`, and `cancel` sets `refundedCents = paidCents` outright, so the `refundedCents <= paidCents` invariant holds on every path. `Order.replay` rejects a non-array with `TypeError` and otherwise just re-drives `apply`, which is why it reproduces the stepwise snapshot and audit trail exactly.

goal.objective:
Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. content.text:
Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

8: /** Error raised for malformed versions, ranges, registries and unsatisfiable graphs. */
9: export class ResolveError extends Error {
10:   /**
11:    * @param {string} code Stable machine-readable reason.
12:    * @param {string} message Human-readable detail.
13:    */
14:   constructor(code, message) {
15:     super(message);
16:     this.name = 'ResolveError';
17:     this.code = code;
18:   }
19: }
20: 
21: const VERSION_PATTERN = /^(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)$/;
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Parse a version string.
25:  *
26:  * @param {string} text Version to parse.
27:  * @returns {{major: number, minor: number, patch: number}} Parsed parts.
28:  */
29: export function parseVersion(text) {
30:   const match = typeof text === 'string' ? VERSION_PATTERN.exec(text) : null;
31:   if (match === null) throw new ResolveError('BAD_VERSION', `invalid version: ${text}`);
32:   return { major: Number(match[1]), minor: Number(match[2]), patch: Number(match[3]) };
33: }
34: 
35: /**
36:  * Order two versions.
37:  *
38:  * @param {string} left First version.
39:  * @param {string} right Second version.
40:  * @returns {-1|0|1} Comparison result.
41:  */
42: export function compareVersions(left, right) {
43:   const a = parseVersion(left);
44:   const b = parseVersion(right);
45:   for (const part of ['major', 'minor', 'patch']) {
46:     if (a[part] !== b[part]) return a[part] < b[part] ? -1 : 1;
47:   }
48:   return 0;
49: }
50: 
51: const VERSION_SOURCE = '(0|[1-9]\\d*)\\.(0|[1-9]\\d*)\\.(0|[1-9]\\d*)';
52: const TOKEN_PATTERN = new RegExp(`^(>=|<=|>|<|=|\\^|~)?${VERSION_SOURCE}$`);
53: 
54: /**
55:  * Parse a range into comparators that must all hold.
56:  *
57:  * @param {string} text Range to parse.
58:  * @returns {Array<{operator: string, version: string}>} Comparators, empty for `*`.
59:  */
60: export function parseRange(text) {
61:   if (typeof text !== 'string') throw new ResolveError('BAD_RANGE', `invalid range: ${text}`);
62:   const trimmed = text.trim();
63:   if (trimmed === '') throw new ResolveError('BAD_RANGE', `invalid range: ${text}`);
64:   if (trimmed === '*') return [];
65:   const tokens = trimmed.split(/\s+/);
66:   if (tokens.includes('*')) throw new ResolveError('BAD_RANGE', `invalid range: ${text}`);
67: 
68:   const comparators = [];
69:   for (const token of tokens) {
70:     const match = TOKEN_PATTERN.exec(token);
71:     if (match === null) throw new ResolveError('BAD_RANGE', `invalid range: ${text}`);
72:     const [, op, majorText, minorText, patchText] = match;
73:     const version = `${majorText}.${minorText}.${patchText}`;
74:     if (op === undefined || op === '=') {
75:       comparators.push({ operator: '=', version });
76:     } else if (op === '>=' || op === '<=' || op === '>' || op === '<') {
77:       comparators.push({ operator: op, version });
78:     } else if (op === '^') {
79:       const major = Number(majorText);
80:       const minor = Number(minorText);
81:       const patch = Number(patchText);
82:       let upper;
83:       if (major > 0) upper = `${major + 1}.0.0`;
84:       else if (minor > 0) upper = `0.${minor + 1}.0`;
85:       else upper = `0.0.${patch + 1}`;
86:       comparators.push({ operator: '>=', version }, { operator: '<', version: upper });
87:     } else {
88:       const major = Number(majorText);
89:       const minor = Number(minorText);
90:       const upper = `${major}.${minor + 1}.0`;
91:       comparators.push({ operator: '>=', version }, { operator: '<', version: upper });
92:     }
93:   }
94:   return comparators;
95: }
96:

98:  * Test a version against a range.
99:  *
100:  * @param {string} version Version to test.
101:  * @param {string} range Range to test against.
102:  * @returns {boolean} True when every comparator holds.
103:  */
104: export function satisfies(version, range) {
105:   parseVersion(version);
106:   const comparators = parseRange(range);
107:   for (const { operator, version: bound } of comparators) {
108:     const cmp = compareVersions(version, bound);
109:     if (operator === '>=' && cmp < 0) return false;
110:     if (operator === '<=' && cmp > 0) return false;
111:     if (operator === '>' && cmp <= 0) return false;
112:     if (operator === '<' && cmp >= 0) return false;
113:     if (operator === '=' && cmp !== 0) return false;
114:   }
115:   return true;

A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. `src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The callable functions are fixed: `abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties toward positive infinity), `sign` take exactly one argument; `pow` and `atan2` take exactly two; `min` and `max` take one or more. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. - **`src/parse.js`** — recursive descent: additive → multiplicative → unary → power → primary. Unary recurses into itself (`--3`, `-+-3`), power's right side parses a unary so `2^-2` works, and since unary sits above power, `-2^2` is -4 while `2^3^2` is right-associative. - **`src/index.js`** — the tree walker. Names resolve through `hasOwnProperty` on `env` first (so `toString`/`constructor` stay unknown) then the constants. `/` and `%` check for a zero divisor before computing; every operation and call result passes through a finiteness check that points at the operator or the call's name. The function table carries min/max arity, driving the singular/plural and "at least" message forms.

Negative zero survives because `-0` is a unary applied to `0`, and `Number.isFinite(-0)` is true, so no normalisation touches it.

Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The callable functions are fixed: `abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties toward positive infinity), `sign` take exactly one argument; `pow` and `atan2` take exactly two; `min` and `max` take one or more. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`.
