goal.objective:
Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Errors are specific. A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Errors are specific. A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

2: import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

4: import { shortestPath, shortestPaths } from '../src/dijkstra.js';
5: 
6: /** Infinity, as it appears in a distance map. */
7: const FAR = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
8: 
9: /**
10:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
11:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
12:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
13:  */
14: function mulberry32(seed) {
15:   let a = seed >>> 0;
16:   return () => {
17:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
18:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
19:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
20:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
21:   };
22: }
23: 
24: /**
25:  * Computes distances with Bellman-Ford as an independent model.
26:  * @param {Record<string, Record<string, number>>} graph Weighted graph.
27:  * @param {string} source Start node.
28:  * @returns {Record<string, number>} Distance per node.
29:  */
30: function bellmanFord(graph, source) {
31:   const nodes = Object.keys(graph);
32:   const dist = {};
33:   for (const node of nodes) dist[node] = FAR;
34:   dist[source] = 0;
35:   for (let round = 0; round < nodes.length; round += 1) {
36:     for (const node of nodes) {
37:       if (dist[node] === FAR) continue;
38:       for (const [target, weight] of Object.entries(graph[node])) {
39:         if (dist[node] + weight < dist[target]) dist[target] = dist[node] + weight;
40:       }
41:     }
42:   }
43:   return dist;
44: }
45: 
46: /** Small hand-checked graph. */
47: const graph = {
48:   a: { b: 1, c: 4 },
49:   b: { c: 2, d: 6 },
50:   c: { d: 3 },
51:   d: {},
52:   island: {},
53: };
54: 
55: test('computes distances and predecessors from one source', () => {
56:   const { dist, prev } = shortestPaths(graph, 'a');
57:   assert.deepEqual(dist, { a: 0, b: 1, c: 3, d: 6, island: FAR });
58:   assert.deepEqual(prev, { a: null, b: 'a', c: 'b', d: 'c', island: null });
59:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPaths(graph, 'c').dist, { a: FAR, b: FAR, c: 0, d: 3, island: FAR });
60:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPaths(graph, 'd').prev, { a: null, b: null, c: null, d: null, island: null });
61: });
62: 
63: test('reconstructs a route or reports that none exists', () => {
64:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPath(graph, 'a', 'd'), { distance: 6, path: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] });
65:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPath(graph, 'a', 'a'), { distance: 0, path: ['a'] });
66:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPath(graph, 'b', 'd'), { distance: 5, path: ['b', 'c', 'd'] });
67:   assert.equal(shortestPath(graph, 'a', 'island'), null);
68:   assert.equal(shortestPath(graph, 'd', 'a'), null);
69: });
70: 
71: test('ties pick the smallest predecessor', () => {
72:   const tie = { s: { m: 2, n: 2 }, m: { t: 3 }, n: { t: 3 }, t: {} };
73:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPaths(tie, 's').prev, { s: null, m: 's', n: 's', t: 'm' });
74:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPath(tie, 's', 't'), { distance: 5, path: ['s', 'm', 't'] });
75:   const flipped = { s: { n: 2, m: 2 }, n: { t: 3 }, m: { t: 3 }, t: {} };
76:   assert.deepEqual(shortestPath(flipped, 's', 't'), { distance: 5, path: ['s', 'm', 't'] });
77: });

80:   const bad = [
81:     [() => shortestPaths(null, 'a'), 'TypeError', 'graph must be an object'],
82:     [() => shortestPaths([{ a: 1 }], 'a'), 'TypeError', 'graph must be an object'],
83:     [() => shortestPaths({ a: ['b'], b: {} }, 'a'), 'TypeError', 'edge map for node "a" must be an object'],
84:     [() => shortestPaths({ a: { q: 1 } }, 'a'), 'ReferenceError', 'unknown node: "q"'],
85:     [() => shortestPaths({ a: { b: 0 }, b: {} }, 'a'), 'RangeError', 'weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"'],
86:     [() => shortestPaths({ a: { b: -2 }, b: {} }, 'a'), 'RangeError', 'weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"'],
87:     [() => shortestPaths({ a: { b: '3' }, b: {} }, 'a'), 'RangeError', 'weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"'],
88:     [() => shortestPaths(graph, 'zz'), 'ReferenceError', 'unknown node: "zz"'],
89:     [() => shortestPath(graph, 'a', 'zz'), 'ReferenceError', 'unknown node: "zz"'],
90:     [() => shortestPaths(graph, 7), 'TypeError', 'source must be a string'],
91:   ];
92:   for (const [call, name, message] of bad) assert.throws(call, { name, message }, message);
93: });

95: test('agrees with Bellman-Ford on random weighted graphs', () => {
96:   const rnd = mulberry32(0xd1357a);
97:   for (let round = 0; round < 60; round += 1) {
98:     const size = 5 + Math.floor(rnd() * 8);
99:     const ids = Array.from({ length: size }, (_, i) => `n${String(i).padStart(2, '0')}`);
100:     const random = {};
101:     for (const id of ids) random[id] = {};
102:     for (const from of ids) {
103:       for (const to of ids) {
104:         if (from !== to && rnd() < 0.3) random[from][to] = 1 + Math.floor(rnd() * 9);
105:       }
106:     }
107:     const source = ids[Math.floor(rnd() * ids.length)];
108:     const { dist, prev } = shortestPaths(random, source);
109:     assert.deepEqual(dist, bellmanFord(random, source), `round ${round}`);
110:     assert.equal(prev[source], null, `round ${round} source predecessor`);
111:     for (const node of ids) {
112:       if (node === source || dist[node] === FAR) {
113:         assert.equal(prev[node], null, `round ${round} ${node} unreachable`);
114:         continue;
115:       }
116:       const candidates = ids.filter((from) => random[from][node] !== undefined && dist[from] + random[from][node] === dist[node]);
117:       assert.equal(prev[node], candidates.sort()[0], `round ${round} predecessor of ${node}`);
118:       const route = shortestPath(random, source, node);
119:       let walked = 0;
120:       for (let i = 1; i < route.path.length; i += 1) walked += random[route.path[i - 1]][route.path[i]];
121:       assert.deepEqual([route.distance, walked, route.path[0]], [dist[node], dist[node], source], `round ${round} route to ${node}`);
122:     }
123:   }
124: });

1: /**
2:  * Binary min-heap with an index from key to position.
3:  *
4:  * This starting point keeps entries in a plain array and scans it to find the
5:  * next one; the index, the ordering guarantees for equal priorities, and the
6:  * keyed operations are missing.
7:  */
8: export class IndexedHeap {
9:   /** @type {Array<{key: string, priority: number}>} */
10:   #items = [];
11: 
12:   /** @returns {number} Number of entries currently held. */
13:   get size() {
14:     return this.#items.length;
15:   }
16: 
17:   /**
18:    * Adds an entry.
19:    * @param {string} key Unique key.
20:    * @param {number} priority Ordering priority; smaller leaves first.
21:    * @returns {void}
22:    */
23:   push(key, priority) {
24:     this.#items.push({ key, priority });
25:   }
26: 
27:   /**
28:    * Reads the next entry without removing it.
29:    * @returns {{key: string, priority: number} | undefined} Next entry, or undefined when empty.
30:    */
31:   peek() {
32:     let best;
33:     for (const item of this.#items) {
34:       if (best === undefined || item.priority < best.priority) best = item;
35:     }
36:     return best === undefined ? undefined : { key: best.key, priority: best.priority };
37:   }
38: 
39:   /**
40:    * Removes and returns the next entry.
41:    * @returns {{key: string, priority: number} | undefined} Next entry, or undefined when empty.
42:    */
43:   pop() {
44:     const next = this.peek();
45:     if (next === undefined) return undefined;
46:     this.#items = this.#items.filter((item) => item.key !== next.key);

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. **What I implemented in `src/trie.js`** (only file changed; no new files, no dependencies):

- **`TrieNode`**: `children` as a `Map` keyed by *code point* (number), plus `terminal`, `value`, and `count` (words at or below the node).

- **`insert`**: creates missing nodes, bumps `nodeCount`; returns the replaced value if the node was already terminal (no count changes), otherwise marks terminal and increments `count` along the whole path.
- **`delete`**: returns `false` for a non-terminal node (a pure prefix), otherwise clears the terminal, decrements path counts, then prunes trailing nodes that are neither terminal nor have children, decrementing `nodeCount`.

`insert(word, value)` stores a value and returns the value it replaced, or `undefined` when the word is new. `get(word)` and `has(word)` read it back. `delete(word)` removes a word, returns whether it removed one, and drops the nodes that word alone kept alive; deleting a string that is only a prefix of stored words removes nothing and returns `false`. `countPrefix(prefix)` returns how many stored words start with the prefix, and must cost the length of the prefix rather than a walk of the subtree, so keep a per-node count of the words below it. `search(prefix, limit)` lists the matching words in order, at most `limit` of them, defaulting to no limit; a prefix that is not in the index yields an empty list. `entries()` lists every `[word, value]` pair in order. `longestPrefixMatch(text)` returns `{ word, value }` for the longest stored word that is a prefix of `text`, or `null` when no stored word is.

Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. `parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so generated postings replay identically. */
6: function mulberry32(seed) {
7:   let a = seed >>> 0;
8:   return function next() {
9:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
10:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
11:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
13:   };
14: }

16: /** A ledger with the five accounts used across these cases. */

18:   const ledger = new Ledger();

21:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'ap', name: 'Payables', type: 'liability' });

What I implemented:

**`src/money.js`**
- `normalSide(type)` — `'debit'` for asset/expense, `'credit'` for liability/equity/income, otherwise `LedgerError('UNKNOWN_TYPE', 'unknown account type: <type>')`.
- `toNormal(type, signedCents)` — delegates to `normalSide` (so it shares the unknown-type check) and negates only for credit-normal types.

**`src/ledger.js`** — added private `#entries` (id → frozen entry) and `#order` (posting order), plus helpers: `checkTime` for non-negative-integer moments, `#cutOff` for `asOf` defaulting to `Infinity`, `#requireAccount`, `#store` (assigns the 1-based `seq`, freezes entry and lines), and `#replace` (frozen copy in place, used to set `reversedBy`).

- `post` validates strictly in the specified order — object, id, duplicate, `at`, `memo`, `lines` array of ≥2, then per line account/integer/non-zero, then the zero-sum check — and only calls `#store` afterwards, so a rejected entry is never stored.
- `entries({ asOf })` filters by the cut-off and sorts by `at` then `seq`, which handles out-of-order posting.
- `balance` keeps the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reuses `toNormal`; `trialBalance` seeds every account at 0 so absent accounts still appear, then splits positives into `debits` and negatives into `credits`.
- `reverse` checks not-found → reversal-of-reversal → already-reversed → id/duplicate → time (including `at < original.at`), then stores the negated lines with the default memo and links both directions. Because the link is written only after `#store` succeeds, a failed reversal leaves `reversedBy` null.
- `statement` walks the full ordered history to accumulate the running balance from the beginning of the ledger, but only emits rows inside the inclusive `from`/`to` window.

goal.objective:
Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). The stored entry is frozen and exposes `id`, `at`, `seq` (its 1-based posting order), `memo`, `lines`, `reverses` and `reversedBy`, the last two null for an ordinary entry. `getEntry(id)` returns it or `undefined`. `entries({ asOf })` returns the entries with `at` at or before the cut-off, ordered by `at` and then by posting order; `asOf` defaults to `Infinity` and must otherwise be a non-negative integer. Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. It throws `'NOT_FOUND'` with message `unknown entry: <id>` for an unknown entry, `'REVERSAL_OF_REVERSAL'` when the target is itself a reversal, `'ALREADY_REVERSED'` with message `entry already reversed: <id>` for a second reversal, and `'BAD_TIME'` when the reversal would precede its entry; a reversal that fails to post leaves the original untouched. `statement(accountId, { from, to })` lists the account's lines inside an inclusive window as `{ entryId, at, seq, amountCents, balanceCents }`, ordered like `entries()`, where `balanceCents` is the running balance counting everything from the beginning of the ledger, not just the window. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. content.text:
Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Errors are specific. A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).

12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };

112: test('matches a naive model across a long random operation sequence', () => {
113:   const rnd = mulberry32(0x1e4d);
114:   const keyPool = Array.from({ length: 24 }, (_, i) => `k${String(i).padStart(2, '0')}`);
115:   const heap = new IndexedHeap();
116:   /** @type {Array<{key: string, priority: number, seq: number}>} */
117:   let model = [];
118:   let seq = 0;
119:   const best = () => {
120:     let winner = null;
121:     for (const item of model) {
122:       if (winner === null || item.priority < winner.priority || (item.priority === winner.priority && item.seq < winner.seq)) {

127:   };

149:       }

163:   }

6: /** Infinity, as it appears in a distance map. */
7: const FAR = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
8: 
9: /**
10:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
11:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
12:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
13:  */
14: function mulberry32(seed) {
15:   let a = seed >>> 0;
16:   return () => {
17:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
18:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
19:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
20:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
21:   };
22: }
23: 
24: /**
25:  * Computes distances with Bellman-Ford as an independent model.
26:  * @param {Record<string, Record<string, number>>} graph Weighted graph.
27:  * @param {string} source Start node.
28:  * @returns {Record<string, number>} Distance per node.
29:  */
30: function bellmanFord(graph, source) {
31:   const nodes = Object.keys(graph);
32:   const dist = {};
33:   for (const node of nodes) dist[node] = FAR;
34:   dist[source] = 0;
35:   for (let round = 0; round < nodes.length; round += 1) {
36:     for (const node of nodes) {
37:       if (dist[node] === FAR) continue;
38:       for (const [target, weight] of Object.entries(graph[node])) {
39:         if (dist[node] + weight < dist[target]) dist[target] = dist[node] + weight;
40:       }
41:     }
42:   }
43:   return dist;
44: }

49:   b: { c: 2, d: 6 },

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

8: /** Error raised for malformed versions, ranges, registries and unsatisfiable graphs. */
9: export class ResolveError extends Error {
10:   /**
11:    * @param {string} code Stable machine-readable reason.
12:    * @param {string} message Human-readable detail.
13:    */
14:   constructor(code, message) {
15:     super(message);
16:     this.name = 'ResolveError';
17:     this.code = code;
18:   }
19: }

21: const VERSION_PATTERN = /^(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)$/;
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Parse a version string.
25:  *
26:  * @param {string} text Version to parse.
27:  * @returns {{major: number, minor: number, patch: number}} Parsed parts.
28:  */
29: export function parseVersion(text) {
30:   const match = typeof text === 'string' ? VERSION_PATTERN.exec(text) : null;
31:   if (match === null) throw new ResolveError('BAD_VERSION', `invalid version: ${text}`);
32:   return { major: Number(match[1]), minor: Number(match[2]), patch: Number(match[3]) };
33: }

35: /**
36:  * Order two versions.
37:  *
38:  * @param {string} left First version.
39:  * @param {string} right Second version.
40:  * @returns {-1|0|1} Comparison result.
41:  */
42: export function compareVersions(left, right) {
43:   const a = parseVersion(left);
44:   const b = parseVersion(right);
45:   for (const part of ['major', 'minor', 'patch']) {
46:     if (a[part] !== b[part]) return a[part] < b[part] ? -1 : 1;
47:   }
48:   return 0;
49: }

goal.objective:
Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
